# What are time series?

## What are time series?

**time series analysis** is a multidisciplinary field: economics, business, finance, physics, life sciences, ...

**examples:**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- business: yearly sales figures, monthly advertising expenditures, ...
- economics: quarterly GDP, monthly price indices, weekly interest rates, ...
- finance: tick-by-tick stock prices, daily currency exchange rates, ...
- agriculture: annual figures for crop and livestock production, soil erosion, export sales, ...
- meteorology: daily high and low temperatures, annual precipitation and drought indices, hourly wind speeds, ...
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- hydrology: hourly river levels, ...
- medicine: electrical activity of the heart at millisecond intervals, ...
:::

::::

## What are time series?

:::{.clean-box}
**time series:** data obtained from observations collected sequentially over time

**notation:** observations $y_t$, at time $t = 1, \dots, T$
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
**some terminology.** We focus on

- **univariate** vs. multivariate
- **regular (equidistant)** vs. irregular
- **discrete time** vs. continuous time
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
**goals of time series analysis**

- [modeling]{.alert}: understand or model the stochastic mechanism underlying a series
- [forecasting]{.alert}: predict future values of a series based on its own history or on (the history of) other series
- [statistical inference]{.alert}: e.g., does the data suggest an upward trend?
:::

::::

# Time series in econom(etr)ics

## Time series in econom(etr)ics

**types of data in economics**

- cross-section data: data for 5,000 households for the year 2025
- time series data: data for one country over 25 years
- panel data: 5,000 households over 5 years ("micro panel"), or 12 countries over 25 years ("macro panel")

**terminology**

- microeconometrics: cross-sectional data and micro panels
- macroeconometrics: time series data and macro panels

## Time series in econom(etr)ics

- Nobel Prize in Economics (actually "Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel") in 2003 went to two "time series econometricians":
  - *Robert F. Engle III* ("for methods of analyzing economic time series with time-varying volatility (ARCH)")
  - *Clive W.J. Granger* ("for methods of analyzing economic time series with common trends (cointegration)")

  see also <https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2003/summary/>

- Thomas J. Sargent and especially Christopher A. Sims (2011) may be seen as time series econometricians

# Examples

## Time series data sets in R packages

- `AirPassengers`: monthly airline passenger numbers (in thousands) from 1949(1) to 1960(12), from Box & Jenkins (1976)
- `UKDriverDeaths`: monthly totals of car drivers in Great Britain killed or seriously injured from 1969(1) to 1984(12)
- `bev`: annual Beveridge Wheat Price Index, 1500 to 1869
- `MarkPound`: daily DEM/GBP exchange rate returns (in %) from 1984-01-03 through 1991-12-31
- `USMacroG`: quarterly US macroeconomic variables (e.g., income, consumption, ...) from 1950(1) to 2000(4), from Greene (2003)
- `PepperPrice`: average monthly European spot prices for black and white pepper (USD/ton) from 1973(10) to 1996(4)
- `EuStockMarkets`: daily closing prices (in business days) of major European stock indices: DAX, SMI, CAC, FTSE

`bev` is from **tseries**. `MarkPound`, `USMacroG`, `PepperPrice` are from **AER**. the rest is from base R.

## Examples: French mortality

```{r frmort-code}
#| eval: false
library("demography")  # fr.mort: French mortality data (HMD), 1816-2006
fr <- extract.ages(extract.years(fr.mort, 1899:2006), 0:95)
lr <- log(fr$rate$total)
cols <- colorRampPalette(c("#08306b", "#c6dbef"))(length(fr$year))
matplot(fr$age, lr, type = "l", lty = 1, col = cols, xlab = "Age",
  ylab = "Log death rate", main = "Total death rates, France 1899-2006")
lines(fr$age, lr[, 1], lty = 2, lwd = 2.5)
lines(fr$age, lr[, ncol(lr)], lty = 2, lwd = 2.5)
idx <- round(seq(1, length(fr$year), length.out = 5))
legend("bottomright", legend = c(fr$year[idx], "first / last year"),
  col = c(cols[idx], "black"), lty = c(rep(1, 5), 2), lwd = c(rep(2, 5), 2.5),
  title = "year", bty = "n")
```

## Examples: METR time horizon of AI agents

```{r metr-code}
#| eval: false
library("yaml")
metr <- read_yaml("https://metr.org/assets/benchmark_results_1_1.yaml")$results
th <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(sapply(metr, `[[`, "release_date")),
  p50 = sapply(metr, function(m) m$metrics$p50_horizon_length$estimate))
th <- th[order(th$date), ]
plot(th$date, th$p50, log = "y", pch = 19, yaxt = "n", xlab = "Model release date",
  ylab = "", main = "METR: 50% time horizon of AI agents")
axis(2, at = c(0.1, 1, 10, 60, 480), labels = c("6 sec", "1 min", "10 min", "1 h", "8 h"), las = 1)
fit <- lm(log(p50) ~ date, data = th)
lines(th$date, exp(fitted(fit)), col = "slategray", lwd = 2)
```

## Examples: METR time horizon of AI agents

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="32%"}
**METR (2025, 2026):** how long are the tasks that AI agents can do?

- tasks: software and research tasks, timed by human experts
- [50% time horizon]{.alert}: task length (in human time) at which a model succeeds with 50% probability
- one observation per model, at its release date: irregular series
- log scale, fitted line: exponential trend, doubling roughly every 6 months

# Data features

## Data features

examples exhibit certain features (some more than one):

- trend
- season
- structural change: changing trend, changing level, changing season, changing volatility
- volatility
- 'random' fluctuations

time series analysis is concerned with modeling, extracting, removing, etc. such features

# Data transformations

## Data transformations

**operators in time series analysis:**

- backshift operator $B$ (also called lag operator, then denoted $L$): $\quad B y_t = y_{t-1}$
- differencing operator $\Delta := 1 - B$: $\quad \Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$
- seasonal differencing operator $\Delta_S := 1 - B^S$: $\quad \Delta_S y_t = y_t - y_{t-S}$

**examples:**

a. macroeconomics: often quarterly or monthly data ($S = 4$ or $S = 12$)
b. finance: returns (continuous or "log returns") are $\quad \Delta \log y_t = \log y_t - \log y_{t-1}$

## Data transformations: The return zoo

**example:** many time series in economics and finance are positive (prices, etc.). often consider [returns]{.alert}

- there are several definitions for returns

- **'returns in continuous time'** or 'continuously compounded returns': 
$$r_t := \Delta \log y_t = \log y_t - \log y_{t-1}$$
    
    - growth at constant rate $r$ compounded continuously over one period gives $y_t = y_{t-1} e^{r}$, hence $r = \log(y_t / y_{t-1}) = r_t$
    - sometimes called *log-returns* because it is the log of the gross return $y_t/y_{t-1}$
    - warning: differencing and taking logs must not be interchanged! $\Delta \log y_t \neq \log \Delta y_t$

- **net returns** are fractional changes in the level: 
$$R_t := \frac{y_t - y_{t-1}}{y_{t-1}} = \frac{y_t}{y_{t-1}} - 1$$
   - also called arithmetic returns
   - note that $R_t \geqslant -1$

---

- **gross returns**: 
$$\mathcal R_t := 1 + R_t = \frac{y_t}{y_{t-1}}$$

   - note that $r_t = \log(\mathcal R_t)$

- returns can often be modeled by a stationary process (see illustration below)

## Data transformations: Illustration

download SMI data directly from the Web using `get.hist.quote()` from (old) package **tseries** and obtain returns:

```{r smi-code}
#| eval: false
library("tseries")
smi <- get.hist.quote(instrument = "^ssmi",
  start = "2017-01-01", end = "2025-08-31",
  quote = "Close", provider = "yahoo", compression = "d",
  retclass = "zoo", quiet = TRUE, drop = FALSE)
lsmi <- log(smi)
dlsmi <- diff(lsmi)  # returns
rsmi <- 100 * dlsmi  # percentage returns
names(rsmi) <- "rsmi"
plot(merge(smi, lsmi, rsmi), main = "",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = c("prices", "log-prices", "returns"))
```

other packages: **quantmod**, **Quandl**, **FredR**, **yfR**, ...

## Data transformations

**advantages of operator notation?** Sometimes this abstraction simplifies notation or computation. 

**example:** (multiple backshifts)
$$B^2 y_t = B(B y_t) = B y_{t-1} = y_{t-2}$$
analogously, $B^k, B^{-k}, B^0, \dots$

**example:** (second differences)
$$\Delta^2 y_t = \Delta(\Delta y_t) = \Delta(y_t - y_{t-1}) = \Delta y_t - \Delta y_{t-1} = y_t - 2 y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}$$
or simply
$$\Delta^2 y_t = (1 - B)^2 y_t = (1 - 2B + B^2) y_t = y_t - 2 y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}$$

**later:** models are written with polynomials in the lag operator, e.g. AR(1): $\quad (1 - \phi B)\, y_t = e_t$



# Time series modeling

## Time series modeling: Sampling of time series observations

::: {style="font-size: 1.25em; margin-bottom: 1em;"}

| | cross-section | time series |
|:------|:------------------|:------------------|
| **sample space** | $\mathbb{R}^n$, one value per unit | $\mathbb{R}^T$, one value per date: a [path]{.alert} |
| **sample** | $y_1, \dots, y_n$, [independent]{.alert} draws, exchangeable | $y_1, \dots, y_T$: [one draw]{.alert} of one path, [dependent]{.alert}, not exchangeable |
| **example** | income of 5,000 households in 2025 | Swiss GDP over 25 years |
| **repeatable?** | yes, draw another household | no, history happens once |

:::

Notes:

- time series samples are not exchangeable: observed time series (0,1,2) is different from (0,2,1)
- statistical inference from one path needs additional structure
  - stability over time: properties we want to estimate need to be stable
  - dependence limited: larger samples (longer paths) provide additional information

## Example: Estimate a mean

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**cross-section**

- $y_i \sim N(\mu, 1)$ i.i.d., $i = 1, \dots, n$
- sample mean $\bar y = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n y_i$
- $\bar y \sim N(\mu, 1/n)$, hence $\bar y \to \mu$ as $n \to \infty$
- every new household adds information
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**time series**

- $y_t \sim N(\mu_t, 1)$, $t = 1, \dots, T$
- sample mean $\bar y = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T y_t$
- target? $\quad \bar y \to \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mu_t$?
- does the limit [exist]{.alert}? does $\bar y$ [converge]{.alert} to it?
  - needs stability
:::

::::

**counterexample: dependence unlimited.** $y_1 \sim N(\mu, 1)$, $\quad y_t = y_{t-1}$ for $t = 2, \dots, T$

- every $y_t \sim N(\mu, 1)$: mean, variance stable over time
- but $\bar y = y_1$ for every $T$: no convergence, a longer path adds [no]{.alert} information
- reason: perfect dependence

**needed:** stability *and* limited dependence (later: stationarity, ergodicity)

## Time series modeling: Outline

- in introductory econometrics: data were assumed to be [independent]{.alert} (or at least [uncorrelated]{.alert})

- in time series analysis: goal is to model [dependence]{.alert}

**outline of time series modeling:**

- consider observed time series as realizations of random variables.

    - we observe a sequence of observations, hence a model must involve a sequence of random variables. 
    - such models are called [stochastic processes (SPs)]{.alert}
    
- need to impose some structure on SP. 
    - e.g. a [stationary stochastic process]{.alert} (constant mean, variance, and other moments)
    - later: extensions, mainly trend-stationary and difference-stationary processes

- for estimation and forecasting: need specific models of stationary stochastic processes.
    - simplest model with dependence: the [**autoregressive process of order 1, AR(1)**]{.alert}
    - later: richer model classes, models for trends, seasonality, and volatility

## Time series modeling: AR(1) process

**AR(1) process:** today's value is a fraction of yesterday's value plus a random shock
$$y_t = \phi \, y_{t-1} + e_t, \qquad \{e_t\} \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
:::{.clean-box}
**white noise:** $\{e_t\} \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)$ if for all $t$ and all $s \neq t$

- $E[e_t] = 0$ (constant mean)
- $\mathrm{Var}(e_t) = \sigma^2$ (constant variance)
- $\mathrm{Cov}(e_t, e_s) = 0$ (uncorrelated)
:::

- no distributional assumption, no independence (only uncorrelated)
- stronger: Gaussian white noise $e_t \sim_{iid} \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)$; for Gaussian $e_t$, uncorrelated and independent coincide
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**questions:**

- when is this process 'stable'?
- how to extract properties (e.g., dependence structure) from the defining equation?
- how to estimate $\phi$?
- how to forecast $y_{t+\ell}$, given present and past $y_t, y_{t-1}, \dots$?
- for which types of data is it suitable?

:::

::::

## Time series modeling: Model selection


**steps:** search for model through iteration of

1. **model specification**: select classes of potentially appropriate models

    - employ visualizations, summary statistics, and subject-matter knowledge
    - principle of parsimony ("Everything should be made as simple as possible but not simpler")

2. **model fitting**: estimate the parameters of the model from the observed series

    - e.g., via least squares (LS) or maximum likelihood (ML)

3. **model diagnostics**: does the model fit the data reasonably well?

    - if not, go back to (1)

# How to study effectively?

## How to study effectively?

comes last, because it is the most important point today

**time series analysis is relatively abstract**

- do not binge, study regularly
- reiterate. rest and sleep in between. it gets easier each time
- your mind is not a computer: reiterate in different forms
- if you are stuck, change perspective and find the simplest thing you can understand. ask. sometimes just formulating the question helps
- do not just sit there and read or watch: summarize slides, try the exercises without looking at the solutions, ...

## If you go on a journey, take someone with you

**form study groups (2–5 persons)**

- easier to get started and more fun
- meet and discuss the lecture or try the exercises together
- ask on the course forum for others that are interested
- study groups also make sense if experience differs: explaining and asking are both very effective

# Software

## Software

**general remarks:** 

- there are many different statistics/econometrics software packages with time series functionality. 

- the base R system ships with many classical time series methods (estimation and simulation of ARIMA models, computation of autocorrelations, ...)

- I will show the code of my plots (but you do not need to learn this part)

    - for programming: focus on the exercises
    
## AI support

- current AI models are extremely helpful for coding

**helpful things:**

- give appropriate context (e.g., student of economics, using R, prefer base R over tidy code, etc.)
- ask it to explain code (probably a good idea to share the respective slides)

## Software: R packages

some CRAN packages for time series analysis:

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- **forecast**: methods for (automatic) forecasting
- **tseries**: time series and financial econometrics
- **tsbox**: class-agnostic time series. for conversion of ts classes
- **urca**: unit roots and cointegration analysis
- **strucchange**: testing, monitoring, and dating structural changes
- **Rmetrics**: collection of packages for financial econometrics (e.g., **fGarch**)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- **rugarch**: univariate GARCH models
- **AER**: data accompanying Kleiber & Zeileis (2008)
- **astsa**: data and functions for Shumway & Stoffer (2017, 2019)
- **TSA**: data and functions for Cryer & Chan (2008). *warning:* **TSA** redefines several base R functions!
:::

::::

**more:** CRAN task view on time series <https://CRAN.R-project.org/view=TimeSeries>

## Software: Time series classes

**data classes:** standard time series class in R is `"ts"`

- aimed at regular series (annual, quarterly, monthly)
- a `"ts"` object is either a numeric vector (univariate series) or a numeric matrix (multivariate series)
- `"tsp"` attribute reflects **t**ime **s**eries **p**roperties: a vector of length 3 with `start`, `end`, and `frequency`. can be queried via `tsp()`


```{r tsp}
#| eval: false
tsp(AirPassengers)
start(AirPassengers)
end(AirPassengers)
```
- create via `ts()`: supply data (numeric vector or matrix) plus arguments `start`, `end`, and `frequency`
- methods for standard generic functions: `plot()`, `lines()`, `str()`, `summary()`, ...
- additional time-series-specific methods: `lag()`, `diff()`, ...

## Example: ts in R

create a quarterly series from five numbers, starting in the second quarter of 2021:

```{r ts-example}
values <- c(1, 3, 4, 7, 17) # create example values
y <- ts(values, start = c(2021, 2), frequency = 4) # create ts object
y
tsp(y)
```

then plot

```{r ts-plot-code}
#| eval: false
y <- ts(c(1, 3, 4, 7, 17), start = c(2021, 2), frequency = 4)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # two panels side by side
plot(y, type = "o", main = "level")
plot(log(y), type = "o", main = "log")
```

## Software: Time series classes

**drawbacks:**

- only numeric time stamps (i.e., not date/time objects)
- missing values cannot be omitted (start/end/frequency no longer sufficient for reconstructing all time stamps!) – a problem with irregular series, e.g., with many financial time series

**R packages for irregular series:** several, we sometimes use **zoo**
